_comment: Correctness sweep: every (rows x cols) cell is run once per entry in
lr_param_sets, so the Rust kernel is compared against scikit-learn across a
range of initialisation parameters rather than a single one. measure_time is
false because this run cares about agreement, not wall-clock.
sklearn_solver: lbfgs only supports l2, so l1_ratio > 0 uses saga to keep both
implementations on the same objective (saga cells are noticeably slower).
The full hyper-parameter space of interest is C in {1, 0.1, 0.01}, fit_intercept
in {true, false}, l1_ratio in [0, 1], tol in {1e-3, 1e-4, 1e-5} and max_iter in
{100, 500, 1000}. The cross product would be 162 parameter sets x 9 grid cells,
so this config keeps the three sets that carry the most information per run:
1. baseline        - the reference point every other set is read against, and
simultaneously the C = 1 / pure-L2 / intercept-on corner.
Any disagreement here is a plain kernel bug, not an
interaction, which is why it has to be measured first.
2. elasticnet_half - l1_ratio = 0.5 is the only set that leaves the pure-L2
objective. It activates the non-smooth L1 term, i.e. the
proximal / soft-threshold branch of the kernel that no
other configuration reaches, so it is the single set most
likely to expose a wrong penalty derivation.
3. weighted_strong_reg - the compound stress set. It carries per-sample
weights (the only set that does), and at the same time
moves C to the far end of the scale (0.01, penalty
dominates the likelihood) and switches the bias term off.
Weights and C are checked together on purpose: both enter
the objective as a scaling of the data term against the
penalty, so a kernel that forgets to normalise by the
weight sum only diverges visibly once the penalty is
large. fit_intercept = false is folded in here because it
needs no separate cell to be conclusive: the coefficient
vector is compared elementwise anyway, and a kernel that
fits a bias regardless shows up immediately in param_mae.
Dropped axes and why. tol and max_iter are left at the strict end (1e-4 / 1000)
in all three sets rather than being swept: they do not change the objective, only
how close each solver gets to it, so a loose-convergence cell reports a
disagreement between two different iterates of the *same* correct optimum. That
is expected behaviour, not a correctness signal, and it would make the weighted
set ambiguous -- a mismatch could not be attributed to the weighting rather than
to an early stop. Sweeping them belongs in the timing run, not here.
C = 0 (as listed in the report's scale) is not runnable: scikit-learn requires
C > 0 and the adapter derives its penalties as 1/C, so 0 would divide by zero.
C = 0.01 is the smallest valid point on that scale and stands in for it.
sample_weight: a set carrying this key is fitted with a per-sample weight vector
of length n_train instead of the unweighted default, passed to BOTH
implementations (the adapter's fit takes sample_weight, and so does
scikit-learn's). kind = lognormal draws w = exp(sigma * N(0, 1)) from a generator
seeded with random_state, which spreads the weights over roughly a decade while
keeping them positive and reproducible. Per-sample rather than per-class values
are used deliberately: a two-valued weight vector is still matched by a kernel
that only tracks a class-level scale factor, a continuous one is not. The Rust
fast path needs float32 C-contiguous weights (see the adapter's
_check_before_fit), so cast them like the X / y arrays or the cell silently falls
back to scikit-learn and rust_fastpath goes false.

lr_param_sets._axis: reference point; C = 1, pure L2, intercept on, tight convergence
lr_param_sets.name: baseline

lr_param_sets._axis: sample weights + C: 1.0 -> 0.01 + fit_intercept: true -> false
lr_param_sets.name: weighted_strong_reg
